title: Liquidity, Volatility, and a Dangerous Calm in Markets - Systematic Investor - Ep.355

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Liquidity, Volatility, and a Dangerous Calm in Markets - Systematic Investor - Ep.355.docx

speakers: Alan Dunne (Dunne/Archive Capital, systematic macro commentator)
summary: Weekly Systematic Investor episode (Jul 2025): trend-following H1 2025 performance update, bond/fiscal macro view, and review of Man and Capstone papers on whether trend following drawdowns are different this time. Conclusion: current drawdown is statistically normal; combine long-vol (first responder) with trend (second responder); family-office portfolios look diversified but are mostly equity beta.

coverage.note: intro, sponsor boilerplate; fastest S&P recovery from 20% drawdown (57 days) vs 1998 and Covid, Fed stimulus context
Denmark/EU, budget bill; trend index performance June/July 2025 (SG Trend, BTOP50, short-term traders), oil shock hurting trend followers
asset class returns, June moves (platinum, coffee), dollar trend, realized vol decline; start of macro bond view
fiscal deficit vs unemployment structural shift, Barry Eichengreen, UK welfare U-turn, fiscal addiction
higher yields thesis, Fed chair risk, long-end bond outflows, Treasury bill issuance, dollar weakness is hedging not selling (BIS)
Man paper 'Trend following and drawdowns: is this time different': strategies that stopped working, SG trend drawdown stats
probability of drawdown for 0.5 Sharpe strategy, crowding as share of futures volume, timing out of drawdowns fails, narratives vs statistics
macro-scenario forecasting of trend performance is hard, 2022; counts of rolling 12m returns above +15% vs below -15%, track-record length
long track records and drawdown probability, CTA share of hedge fund AUM down from 27% to 6%, crowding rebutted, interest in index
drawdown perception, 2022 once-in-career rate trade; Capstone paper hero to villain: long vol first responder, trend second responder
long-vol vs trend blend; UBS Global Family Office report, 'looks diversified acts like beta'
family office allocation critique, survey results (hedge funds, gold, risks, challenges), episode wrap-up

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - first reader caught nearly all mechanisms and the paper statistics; missed the post-recovery analogue outcome, Eichengreen's view, several behavioral/allocator points and the hedge-fund convexity caveat.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it was the fastest recovery from a 20% draw down for the S&P 500 um in in the last number of decades since the post-war period
claims.claim: The S&P 500 recovered a 21% drawdown to new highs in 57 days in 2025, faster than Covid and the 1998 LTCM episode (61 days); both earlier rebounds coincided with Fed easing, this one did not, which points to a strong buy-the-dip mentality and bullish sentiment.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 drawdown recovery time
claims.direction: equities rally continued about a year after both earlier fast rebounds
claims.testable: yes: drawdown-recovery speed vs forward 12m returns is testable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: The simple conclusion of course is the less the does the quicker the rebound
claims.claim: Without Fed stimulus the rebound was even quicker, so fast V-shaped recoveries do not require policy support when dip-buying sentiment is strong.
claims.testable: partly: needs a sample of rebounds with and without stimulus

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: my trim router finished at 57 yesterday. That's a rise over the last 10 days and that probably corresponds well with what's happened in the industry
claims.claim: A proprietary trend-following router/proxy finished at 57 after a 10-day rise, in line with improving CTA industry performance in late June.
claims.indicator: Alan Dunne trend router (as reported)

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the C02 market update (incl. 'my trim router finished at 57') is given by the host Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, not Alan Dunne; 'trim router' is a caption error for his trend barometer.
correction.fix: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen's trend barometer finished at 57 after a 10-day rise, in line with improving CTA performance in late June 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: surprise attack on Iran that sent oil prices surging catching I think a lot of trend followers on the wrong side
claims.claim: The June 2025 surprise attack on Iran spiked oil and caught short-oil trend followers wrong-footed; those who exited the shorts then got no benefit from the oil collapse days later, so geopolitical energy shocks whipsaw trend portfolios.
claims.indicator: crude oil
claims.conditions: reversal within days after US involvement
claims.testable: partly: event study of trend returns around geopolitical spikes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the B top 50 index has started out July up 30 basis points uh still down 3.1 16% for the year
claims.claim: CTA indices were negative in 2025 at July: BTOP50 about -3.2%, SG Trend about -7.8%, SG CTA -10%/short-term traders -5.15% YTD, while MSCI World was +9.5%, bonds +3.4%, S&P 500 +6.8%.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG Trend Index, SG Short-Term Traders Index, MSCI World, S&P 500

correction.issue: Indices likely swapped: the caption reads SG CTA index (garbled 'Stockton trend sorry in CT index') down 7.8% YTD and SG Trend index down 10% YTD, not SG Trend -7.8% and SG CTA -10%; BTOP50 is -3.16%.
correction.fix: At early July 2025: BTOP50 -3.16% YTD, SG CTA index about -7.8%, SG Trend index about -10%, SG short-term traders -5.15%; MSCI World +9.5%, US aggregate bonds +3.44%, S&P 500 +6.76%.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: doesn't seem to have benefited uh shortterm models uh as much as you might think in a rangebound uh erratic market
claims.claim: Short-term trend models did not benefit from the quick market reversals, and on a vol-adjusted basis performed about as badly as the longer-term SG Trend index, so faster speeds were no protection in the choppy 2025 market.
claims.indicator: SG Short-Term Traders Index vs SG Trend Index
claims.conditions: range-bound erratic markets hurt long-term managers

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: platinum up uh almost 27% in uh in June and and uh I think according to uh some long-term uh time frames breaking out to the upside
claims.claim: Platinum rose about 27% in June 2025 and broke out on long-term trend horizons while coffee fell 12% and cocoa also dropped, showing large idiosyncratic commodity swings that trend models can capture or miss depending on speed.
claims.indicator: platinum, coffee, cocoa prices

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the trend in the dollar was probably a dominant theme you know particularly against European currencies euro up you know above 117
claims.claim: The dollar downtrend (euro above 1.17, Swiss franc at multi-year lows against the dollar) was a dominant positive contributor to trend managers in June 2025.
claims.indicator: USD vs EUR, CHF, GBP

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: realize volatility has come down quite a bit um in where you can track daily return data
claims.claim: Realized volatility of trend managers fell after the April 2025 spike because positions were scaled back and resized, which is the vol-targeting response to a volatility spike.
claims.indicator: realized volatility of managers' daily returns
claims.direction: reduced position sizes after vol spike

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I wrote a piece um all roads lead to higher yields
claims.claim: Fiscal, term-premium and supply factors all point to higher long-term bond yields, although yields had corrected about 50bp from highs in mid-2025 on Fed-cut expectations (Waller, Bowman) and a flatter curve.
claims.indicator: long-end Treasury yields, term premium
claims.conditions: near term yields fell on dovish Fed governors
claims.testable: partly: the long-run direction is a view, not a rule

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: is the curve steener um maybe widely held in the market. Maybe it's it's a trade a lot of people have on
claims.claim: The calm bond market reaction to the budget bill may reflect that the curve-steepener trade was already widely held, so the news was priced in.
claims.indicator: yield curve slope (steepener positioning)

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you basically look at the relationship on an annual basis between the fiscal deficit and the level of unemployment. It's a pretty clear relationship historically
claims.claim: Historically the fiscal deficit rises with unemployment (recessions cut revenues and raise welfare), but there has been a structural shift: deficits of 7-8% of GDP once signalled crisis and now coexist with near full employment.
claims.indicator: US fiscal deficit vs unemployment rate
claims.direction: higher structural deficits, more Treasury supply
claims.testable: yes: annual deficit-unemployment regression and residual

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if we do see weaker economic growth, that probably does take the heat out of the bond market in terms of, you know, fears of higher bond yields in the short term
claims.claim: A growth slowdown would temporarily relieve bond yield pressure but widen the deficit further, so the supply pressure returns in the subsequent recovery.
claims.indicator: long Treasury yields, deficit
claims.conditions: recessions lower yields short term; yields pressure after recovery

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: there is zero appetite for for for austerity
claims.claim: Political appetite for austerity is nil (UK welfare reform reversed; US bill passed), a fiscal addiction that stems from a decade of zero rates and COVID spending, so deficits are not likely to be cut and the risks are higher yields and taxes.
claims.indicator: fiscal policy reversals (UK welfare U-turn)

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: all it takes is just a one influential chair to tilt the narrative, tilt the balance of the discussion towards a much more dovish Fed
claims.claim: A Trump-appointed dovish Fed chair, even as one vote, could tilt the FOMC toward cuts, which would be negative for the long end of the bond market via inflation/term-premium risk.
claims.indicator: Fed chair appointment

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: highlighting the outflows from the long end of the uh US um bond market. So I think it was about 11 billion in in in um in outflows of long-term bonds
claims.claim: FT reported roughly $11 billion of outflows from long-dated government and corporate bonds, a bearish demand signal not yet reflected in yields; the supplementary leverage ratio change (banks hold less capital against Treasuries) is a possible offset.
claims.indicator: long-term bond fund flows; supplementary leverage ratio

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: issuance has been pretty low so far this year. So I would imagine they would have to issue a lot more extra treasuries probably bills uh um in the autumn
claims.claim: Low Treasury issuance early in 2025 plus the new bill implies heavy extra bill issuance in autumn, which should pressure rates higher and may support the dollar after its worst calendar-year start in 50 years.
claims.indicator: Treasury issuance, bill supply

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they concluded it was more hedging pressure than actual sales of dollar assets
claims.claim: The BIS found that 2025 dollar weakness reflected hedging of US assets (selling in Asian hours, cross-currency basis widening) rather than outright foreign selling of US assets, so the 'end of US exceptionalism' trade may only be beginning if at all.
claims.indicator: BIS report, cross-currency basis, timing of dollar selling by time zone
claims.testable: yes: cross-currency basis and intraday flow patterns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: for sure there have been some systematic strategies that over time have seen a deterioration in performance and effectively stopped working
claims.claim: The Man paper distinguishes strategies that have decayed (pairs trading since the 2000s, fast trend following since the 70s-80s) from ones with tough but recoverable drawdowns (equity-factor long-short, trend following), arguing trend following is in the second group.
claims.indicator: pairs trading, fast trend following, equity factor long-short
claims.testable: yes: subperiod Sharpe ratios by strategy

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: only twice has the sock gen trend index been down more than 15% over 12 months
claims.claim: SG Trend Index has been down more than 15% over 12 months only twice in 25 years (about -16% in January 2019, followed by a big rebound), and the current -18% 1-year drawdown is rare but not outside history.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index rolling 12-month return

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the riskreward profile is is is is better or at least the downside is better managed in risk in in in in trend following
claims.claim: Trend-following losses are smaller than equity drawdowns, so the risk/reward profile is better managed than equities even in bad years.
claims.indicator: trend following vs equity drawdown

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: normally up kind of around 10% after being down in a 10% draw down
claims.claim: Trend index returns after a 10% drawdown have typically been around +10% over the following period, and January 2019 to May 2024 was a particularly strong rebound.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index returns after drawdowns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the probability of a 20% draw and is nearly 80%
claims.claim: A 0.5 Sharpe, 10% vol, zero-equity-correlation strategy has a nearly 80% probability of experiencing a 20% drawdown over 25 years, so the 2025 trend drawdown is within statistical expectation.
claims.indicator: drawdown probability as function of Sharpe, vol, horizon

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: CTA volume as a percentage of the overall volume
claims.claim: Crowding concern is rebutted by CTA volume falling as a share of futures volume; caveat that QIS and in-house trend following sits outside the CTA industry numbers.
claims.indicator: CTA volume as share of futures volume
claims.testable: partly: in-house/QIS trend assets are unobservable

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you were to cut it in draw down and then wait for it to come back up you know obviously what they find you know that that doesn't prove to be a good strategy historically
claims.claim: Cutting exposure to trend following (or quant strategies) during drawdowns and waiting for recovery to re-enter loses a lot of return historically, so drawdown-based manager timing does not work.
claims.indicator: drawdown-based allocation switching

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you take a 6 sharp strategy at 15 VA over 30 years um you know over the full 30 years your money would have grown about 8 eightfold
claims.claim: Even a 0.6 Sharpe, 15% vol strategy that grew money about eightfold over 30 years had a 32% drawdown and spent 9 years underwater, so long drawdowns are normal for good strategies.
claims.indicator: simulated 0.6 Sharpe strategy drawdown and underwater period

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: people like stories better than stat statistics
claims.claim: Narratives (choppy markets, tariff on/off) are easy to attach to a drawdown but past choppy periods (2011-12, 2016-19) eventually ended and the cause may just be randomness, so assigning macro narratives to performance is dangerous.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it is a good a good lesson in trying to link expected performance to you know a macro scenario it's just hard to do that
claims.claim: Trend performance cannot be forecast from the macro scenario: 2022 looked set for higher macro volatility, inflation and rates yet 2023-25 had range-bound bonds (10y 3.5-5%) and four recession scares.
claims.indicator: 10-year Treasury yield range 2022-2025
claims.testable: yes: macro regime vs trend return regressions

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Almost 60 times we've had, you know, um rolling 12 month returns of more than uh 15%
claims.claim: In the SG Trend Index over 25 years, rolling 12-month returns above +15% occurred far more often (about 59 times) than below -15% (2 times), so the return distribution is positively skewed.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index rolling 12-month returns

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you're only been in business for 5 years you've actually only got a 21% chance of having experienced this
claims.claim: Probability of having experienced a two-standard-deviation drawdown is 79% over 25 years but only 21% over 5 years, so short track records understate drawdown risk and long track records are more informative.
claims.indicator: probability of drawdown vs track-record length

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it 75% of the managers include interest in all the managers
claims.claim: About 75% of managers include interest in reported returns; removing interest yields a larger drawdown (27-28%) that has not fully recovered since 2024, so index drawdown depends on whether interest is included.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index with and without interest

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Back in the '9s uh they they show it as as high as something like 27% of the AUM
claims.claim: CTA share of hedge-fund AUM fell from about 27% in the 1990s to about 6%, while futures volume rose strongly and CTA AUM stagnated for 20 years, which argues against over-crowding.
claims.indicator: CTA AUM share of hedge fund industry; futures volume
claims.testable: yes: data from BarclayHedge and exchanges

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: This is this is a period where trend following should not work when you look at what markets are doing especially when it happens in the three main financial sectors at the same time
claims.claim: Trend following struggles when reversals hit bonds, currencies and equities simultaneously, so the 2025 losses are explained by choppiness across the three main sectors, not crowding.
claims.indicator: simultaneous reversals across rates, FX, equities

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you are in business the the higher the probability is that you're going to experience something
claims.claim: Strategies with short track records (e.g. last 5 years) look safer simply because they have not yet had time to hit the drawdowns that longer records show.
claims.indicator: track-record length

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the conclusion is is we haven't seen enough uh sustained trends
claims.claim: The cause of the 2025 trend drawdown is a lack of sustained trends in aggregate (despite trends in some markets), after the exceptional 2022 rates trade from near-zero rates.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it was it was kind of a once in a in a career kind of rate adjustment
claims.claim: The 2022 trend gains came from a one-off rate adjustment from zero, with managers positioning early with large size, so 2022 performance should not be extrapolated.
claims.indicator: global short rate cycle 2022

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: first first responders and second responders with um you know the being a potential role in the portfolio for long volatility strategies as a first responder solution and then um trend following as a second responder
claims.claim: The Capstone paper argues long-volatility strategies protect in sudden crashes (first responder, e.g. March 2020) and trend following protects in prolonged declines (second responder, e.g. 2022), so a blend is more robust.
claims.indicator: long volatility vs trend following in equity drawdowns
claims.testable: yes: test in a set of drawdown episodes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: equities go down but hey there's no protection from vault because that happened at a very low vault pace
claims.claim: Long-vol strategies gave no protection in 2022 because equities fell from a low-vol starting point and long-vol positions had bled for two years after 2020.
claims.indicator: long volatility strategies
claims.conditions: starting from a low volatility level

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: looks diversified, acts like beta
claims.claim: Family-office portfolios spread across 12 categories (developed/EM equity, private equity, real estate, high yield, EM debt) are mostly equity/growth beta that fails together in stress, with only about 4% in hedge funds and under 1% in commodities.
claims.indicator: UBS Global Family Office Report 2025 allocation
claims.testable: partly: map asset classes to factor betas

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: credit instruments start behaving more like equities just when you want them to behave less like equities
claims.claim: High yield, investment grade and EM debt widen and behave like equity in stress, so fixed income tilted to credit does not diversify equity risk.
claims.indicator: credit spreads vs equity correlation

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: in a stagflationary environment should that reemerge this kind of portfolio is going to struggle
claims.claim: A typical family-office allocation is a bet on favorable growth and stable inflation and lacks commodities and convexity, so it would struggle in stagflation.
claims.indicator: portfolio exposure to growth/inflation regime

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: 38% responded that they're trying to find the right risk offsetting asset or strategy is their biggest challenge
claims.claim: In the UBS survey of 317 family offices (average net worth $2.7bn) 38% rank finding a risk-offsetting asset as their biggest challenge; 20% plan to raise hedge fund allocations and 21% gold; biggest 12-month risk is a global trade war, over 5 years geopolitical conflict.
claims.indicator: UBS Global Family Office Report 2025

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: in those two cases the the rally went on to continue for about a year before we saw the reversal
claims.claim: In both historical analogues of a very fast recovery from a 20% S&P 500 drawdown (1998 and 2020), the rally continued for about a year before reversing, suggesting fast V-shaped recoveries tend to be followed by further gains rather than an immediate relapse.
claims.indicator: days to recover a 20% S&P 500 drawdown
claims.direction: equities up for about a year after a fast recovery to new highs
claims.conditions: only two analogues, both with Fed easing; this time no easing
claims.testable: yes - event study of post-recovery returns, small sample

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: his perspective was at the time that central bankers expected governments to make more progress on um on addressing deficits
claims.claim: Per Barry Eichengreen, central bankers two years earlier expected governments to bring 5-6% of GDP deficits down; instead deficits grew, and he became much more pessimistic, signalling that monetary policy makers cannot count on fiscal consolidation.
claims.indicator: fiscal deficit % of GDP vs official expectations
claims.testable: partly - deficit outcomes vs projections can be tracked; expectations are anecdotal

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the worse the performance gets in our industry, the the the better or the the higher the
claims.claim: The volume of research papers defending trend following rises as CTA performance worsens, so a wave of such papers is itself a marker of a deep industry drawdown and weak allocator sentiment.
claims.indicator: count of manager papers on trend-following drawdowns
claims.testable: partly - paper counts vs SG Trend drawdown could be compiled

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: If you're already suspicious uh skeptical you're probably not going to change your mind on the back back of it because you're you're probably going to be seduced by the narrative.
claims.claim: Statistical evidence that a drawdown is normal rarely changes skeptical allocators' minds; staying invested in trend following requires a prior conviction that the strategy works over time, which is why allocators often exit in drawdowns.
claims.testable: partly - CTA flows vs trailing performance

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: there was a sense that trend following went mainstream I was hearing you know people talking about allocating to trend following who had never said that before
claims.claim: After the strong 2022 year trend following went mainstream with new allocators, and the sentiment shift now (doubt among those same investors) is notable: performance-chasing allocators arrive after the best year and lose faith in the following drawdown.
claims.indicator: allocator interest in trend following after strong years
claims.conditions: after an exceptional year such as 2022
claims.testable: partly - CTA AUM flows after strong and weak years

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: managers that they've probably had even more negative experiences. So, so that will that will um influence the perception of of certain investors
claims.claim: Individual CTA managers have had worse drawdowns than the index, so investors holding only one or two managers experience the strategy's bad periods more severely than index statistics suggest; manager dispersion shapes perception and the case for diversifying across managers.
claims.indicator: dispersion of single-manager returns vs SG Trend Index
claims.testable: yes - compare single-manager vs index drawdown distributions

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe combining them makes sense. I don't know. Um I still like the pure trend approach of course.
claims.claim: Niels is only lukewarm on the long-vol plus trend blend argued by Capstone and Alan, preferring a pure trend approach; a disagreement on whether adding long volatility improves a crisis-hedge portfolio.
claims.testable: yes - compare pure trend vs long-vol/trend blend through equity drawdowns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you have a 4% allocation of hedge funds and they're all low V market neutral funds, you're not going to get much [L440] convexity there in times of stress
claims.claim: A hedge fund allocation only diversifies if it holds divergent strategies run at meaningful volatility; a small allocation to low-vol market-neutral or long-short equity funds adds little convexity in a crisis.
claims.indicator: hedge fund strategy type and volatility level
claims.testable: yes - crisis-period returns by hedge fund strategy and vol

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: 53% who mention that they do worry about a global recession in the [L460] next five years um and then a debt crisis. 50% worries about a debt crisis in the next 5 years as well.
claims.claim: UBS 2025 family office survey: 53% worry about a global recession and 50% about a debt crisis over five years (not over 12 months); 64% of assets are in active strategies vs 36% passive; 29% worry about the predictability of safe-haven assets and 26% about costs and fees.
claims.indicator: UBS Global Family Office Report 2025
